questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss in detail each of the following renewable energy technologies and identify how each contributes to making a home more eco-friendly: • evacuated tubes • wind turbines • photovoltaic panels.

rows.contextNote: 2. Wind turbine

options: Wind activates the turning of the blades and rotor. They spin the main shaft and gearbox, which spins the generator resulting in electrical output
They can be connected to batteries or the national grid

When the wind flows across the blade, the air pressure on one side of the blade decreases. The difference in air pressure across the two sides of the blade creates both lift and drag. The force of the lift is stronger than the drag and this causes the rotor to spin
An inverter is needed to convert the direct current (DC) voltage from the turbine to match the alternating current (AC) voltage required for domestic use
The control box is used to protect the invertor and turbine in strong winds. If the wind becomes too strong the control box will slow the turbine down
If the turbine sits on a tower, then a concrete foundation is generally required
Planning permission may however be required if it is thought that the turbine would interfere with the character of the landscape or a special amenity

rows.contextNote: 3. Photovoltaic cells

options: A photovoltaic panel is a collection of photovoltaic (PV) cells. Multiple panels can be wired together to form an array. In general, the larger the area of a module or array, the more electricity that will be produced

The solar panel system uses particles of light from the sun (photons) to separate electrons from atoms. The process of separating electrons causes the electrons to hit off metal conductor strips on the outside of the PV cells thus generating electricity
Excess electricity can be stored in batteries or sent back to the grid

No waste product is generated

questionText: Describe using notes and freehand sketches, one test that is carried out to determine the airtightness of a house.

rows.verbatim: The blower door test for airtightness
rows.contextNote: The blower door test for airtightness

options: The blower door test is carried out by a trained energy professional

Blower door test consist of: o a frame and flexible panel that fits into a doorway o a variable speed fan o a digital pressure gauge to measure the pressure differences inside and outside the house o a device for measuring airflow, known as a manometer
A powerful fan is mounted into the frame of an exterior doorway
After calibrating the device, the fan pulls air out of the house, lowering the air pressure inside
The higher outside air pressure then flows in through all unsealed gaps, cracks, and openings such as gaps, cracks, or wiring penetrations
If conditions do not allow for lowering the pressure in the home, the fan may also be operated in reverse, with air pressure increased inside the home
While the blower test is being conducted, the analyst may use an infrared camera to look at the walls, ceilings, and floors, to find specific locations where insulation is missing, and air is leaking
The tester may also use a nontoxic smoke pencil to detect air leaks
This determines the air infiltration rate of the house, and the results are recorded on a laptop

options: Solar energy can be turned into electricity using photovoltaic (PV) panels, which converts solar energy/light into electrical energy using silicon cells

The Air to Water (ATW) system has an outdoor unit. Using a fan, the unit takes heat from the air outside and transfers the heat to a coolant liquid which circulated in a closed pipe system
A compressor further increases the temperature of the coolant liquid which transfers the heat to a hot water tank via a heat exchanger
The cooled coolant then returns to the outdoor unit to begin the cycle again
Meanwhile, the newly heated water in the tank is circulated in a separate system to radiators or underfloor heating pipes, heating the house or fused for domestic hot water
Currently Air to Water heat pumps have a “Co-efficiency of Performance” (C.O.P.) of between 3 - 4
Solar evacuated tubes are a type of solar thermal technology that converts sunlight into energy for primarily water heating
The evacuated tubes consist of a glass outer tube and an inner tube with a heat pipe containing a small amount of liquid
The air between the two tubes is evacuated to create a vacuum, which minimizes heat loss due to convection and conduction

questionText: Discuss two advantages of installing triple glazing in a modern window framing system.

rows.contextNote: Advantages

options: Reduced energy costs
Reduced heat loss through the building fabric
Improved acoustic insulation

Reduced condensation. Condensation forms on window panes when excess moisture in the air collides with cold surfaces. Windows are prone to condensation when it is colder outside than inside. To get rid of condensation, ventilation is needed with a subsequent loss in heat

Double glazing reduces thermal transmittance. The inner pane of glass is not as cold as the outside and moisture doesn’t form. Triple glazing can reduce the cold on the inner pane of glass even more with its super thermal efficiency, resulting in less condensation on the inside of windows

questionText: Discuss two disadvantages of installing triple glazing in a modern window framing system.

rows.contextNote: Disadvantages

options: Higher glazing costs. Double glazing is less expensive than triple glazing units. Triple glazing could add up to 30 % to the glazing cost of a building

Overheating issues. If the building design plan includes extensive triple glazing, especially on the southern elevation, overheating can occur during summer months. To counteract overheating, an external solar shading system or an increase in thermal mass internally may have to be installed

Weight issues. Triple glazing units are heavier and difficult to install. Triple glazing may require structural support around the window frame to with-stand the weight. With triple glazing, the added weight means hinges and opening mechanisms need to be more complex, which contributes to their higher cost. Bi-fold doors usually come double glazed due to the glazing weight

Retrofit difficulties. Triple glazing is not suitable for retro fitting into existing door and window frames in most cases. The thickness and weight of the triple glazed units are incompatible with many existing frames so an entire new frame and unit would have to be installed

questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss in detail how each of the following could be improved, when upgrading an existing building to meet the EnerPHit standard: • indoor air quality.

rows.contextNote: Indoor air quality

options: EnerPHit buildings benefit from mechanical ventilation with heat recovery systems (MVHR). These systems ensure a constant supply of fresh air while recovering heat from exhausted air, maintaining energy efficiency. Regular maintenance and filter changes are crucial in keeping systems effective and to ensure fresh air circulation

Selecting building materials, finishes, and furnishing that have low levels of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and other pollutants can significantly improve indoor air quality. This includes paints, adhesives, sealants, and flooring materials designed to emit minimal toxins

Maintaining optimal humidity levels (between 30-50%) helps prevent mould growth which can degrade the indoor air quality. EnerPHit buildings often incorporate humidity-controlled ventilation to keep humidity within this ideal range, especially in bathrooms and kitchens
Continuous monitoring of indoor air quality through sensors and regular maintenance of ventilation systems ensure issues are identified and addressed promptly
Install glazed manual openings in all rooms so that air can naturally circulate bringing in fresh air from the outside and removing stale moist air from the inside

questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss in detail how each of the following could be improved, when upgrading an existing building to meet the EnerPHit standard: • space heating.

rows.contextNote: Space heating

options: Upgrading the insulation in the building envelope is fundamental. High quality continuous insulation in walls, roofs, and floors reduces heat loss

Installing high performing glazing and doors with low U-values minimises heat loss. Properly sealing all openings will ensure the elimination of drafts at the junction of components. This will reduce load and demand on space heating source

Implementing highly efficient heating systems, such as air-source or ground-source heat pumps, will significantly improve space heating efficiency. Heat pumps run at a 5:1 co-efficiency of performance

Using mechanical ventilation with heat recovery ensures heat from outgoing stale air is transferred to incoming fresh air. This reduces the need and demand on additional heating, maintaining a comfortable indoor environment with minimal energy use

Maximising solar gains through passive solar design helps reduce the load on active heating. This involves strategically placing glazing to capture sunlight during winter and using thermal mass materials to store and slowly release heat. Ensuring proper shading and glazing treatments can prevent overheating during warmer months, maintaining a balanced 20 °C indoor temperature
Use PHribbon package to calculate the total cradle-to-grave carbon emitted of constructing new dwellings
Use only products with Environmental Product Declarations (EPD)
The hierarchy for waste management is: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle. Leaner production can reduce the amount of raw materials used
Good architectural and structural design, including use of standard sizes can reduce the amount of material needed and resulting waste in construction

Planning for disassembly at end of building life, allows reuse or recycling. The use of a site waste management plan encourages the contractors and designers to consider all of these issues from the earliest stages of a building project

To enable products and buildings to become more circular, it is important to consider how they are designed. Important considerations for products include designing for disassembly, the potential for standardisation and modularity, the use of secondary materials, avoiding the use of hazardous and composite materials which may hinder reuse and recycling opportunities

For buildings, the way the products are assembled and connected together is important. Using mechanical fixings rather than bonding is preferable, as is making sure that shorter lived products are accessible and are not enclosed by longer life material
Designing for flexibility and adaptability (both in function and form) to enable components and buildings to be used for longer, which avoids the need for new resources
Government and local authorities should support and actively encourage the re-use and repurposing of existing buildings

It is commonly used for heating or cooling indoor spaces and can be more energy-efficient compared to traditional heating and cooling systems
Heat pumps work by extracting heat from a heat source such as the air, water, or ground and transferring it into a home
A heat pump system uses underfloor heating or radiators to transfer heat around the home
A heat pump uses electricity as its main power source, but they generally have a coefficient of performance ratio (COP) of 3-4
Grants are available to homeowners to encourage them to change from a fossil fuel heating system to a heat pump

stem: The external wall of a house built in the 1970s is of single leaf hollow-block construction with an external render. Insulated plasterboard is fixed to the internal surface of the wall. It is proposed to upgrade the thermal properties of the external wall by installing external insulation as shown.
questionText: It has been decided that the wall at 5(a) above should meet the Passive House standard, by further increasing the thickness of the external insulation. Calculate the thickness of additional external insulation required to achieve a U-value of 0.11 W/m2 ºC.

rows.verbatim: Resistance for U-value for 0.11 W/m2 °C (using R=1/U)
rows.contextNote: Required resistance = 1 ÷ 0.11 = 9.091 m²K/W (the scheme first finds R = 1 ÷ 0.221 = 4.525 for the wall at 5(a)).
Additional resistance = 9.091 − 4.525 = 4.566 m²K/W.
R = T ÷ k for the external insulation: 4.566 = T ÷ 0.030.
T = 4.566 × 0.030 = 0.137 m, so 137 mm of additional insulation. Alternative calculation methods are acceptable.

sourceMaterial.attribution: SEC Leaving Certificate Construction Studies 2015 Higher Level — © State Examinations Commission.
sourceMaterial.presentationNote: Original positions A/B, dimensions and south-facing rear wall retained. Both options are compared, then one design option is selected. Scheme drawings are examples, not mandatory designs.

stem: Use the original ground-floor and rear-garden plan of the two-storey semi-detached house. Its external walls are 400 mm concrete block with a full-fill insulated cavity, and rear wall M–M faces south. The owners need an additional study and occasional family space with internal dimensions 5.0 m × 3.0 m. Option A is a single-storey extension attached to the rear of the house at A; option B is a detached, free-standing room in the garden at B. Part (a) compares BOTH options. Part (b) selects ONE option for the external design, internal layout and link to the surrounding rear garden. Part (c) discusses two advantages of linking the room and garden.
questionText:
Discuss in detail two advantages of the attached extension at A.

Discuss in detail two disadvantages of the attached extension at A.

Discuss in detail two advantages of the detached garden room at B.

Discuss in detail two disadvantages of the detached garden room at B.

Select option A: an attached single-storey extension at A. Using notes and freehand sketches, show a proposed external design for the attractive study/family space.

For option A, an attached single-storey extension at A, use notes and freehand sketches to show the proposed internal layout of the 5.0 m × 3.0 m study/family space.

For option A, an attached single-storey extension at A, show in your design how the proposed space links with the surrounding rear garden.

Discuss two advantages of designing a space that links with the rear garden.

rows.verbatim: conserves space in the rear garden of the house
rows.contextNote: Award two distinct, relevant advantages at 3 marks each (6 total). Source examples include conserving rear-garden space; reducing external-wall area and associated insulation costs; easier connection to existing services; flexible division of the combined living space; and closer family/social connection. Discuss each point in relation to this house and location; do not count a repeated point twice. Other relevant, well-argued points remain acceptable. This narrowed practice task retains its own 6 marks; the full comparison requires all four pairs.

rows.verbatim: can reduce the natural lighting and ventilation of the kitchen/dining room
rows.contextNote: Award two distinct, relevant disadvantages at 3 marks each (6 total). Source examples include reducing existing kitchen/dining light or ventilation; disturbing the original layout or views; losing quieter separate rooms; demanding weatherproof and insulated junctions; and structural support needed for a larger opening in the existing external wall. Discuss each point in relation to this house and location; do not count a repeated point twice. Other relevant, well-argued points remain acceptable. This narrowed practice task retains its own 6 marks; the full comparison requires all four pairs.

Award two distinct, relevant advantages at 3 marks each (6 total). Source examples include less disruption; retaining light and views from existing rooms; a separate quiet/private study; more freedom in the new room design; and a direct relationship with the garden. Discuss each point in relation to this house and location; do not count a repeated point twice. Other relevant, well-argued points remain acceptable. This narrowed practice task retains its own 6 marks; the full comparison requires all four pairs.

Award two distinct, relevant disadvantages at 3 marks each (6 total). Source examples include a larger exposed envelope and associated insulation/heating costs; moving outdoors to reach the room; loss of garden space to paths; separating family living space; and extra access or service-connection costs. The scheme heading 3(b)(ii) on PDF page 10 is a numbering error: these are the disadvantages for part(a), option B. Discuss each point in relation to this house and location; do not count a repeated point twice. Other relevant, well-argued points remain acceptable. This narrowed practice task retains its own 6 marks; the full comparison requires all four pairs.

External-design notes 6 and sketches 6 (12 total). Join the extension to the south-facing rear wall M–M at A and keep the specified 5.0 m × 3.0 m internal space. The source suggests a low roof/elevation where appropriate to avoid overshadowing the enclosed garden, south-facing windows for daylight, and an attractive design appropriate to the house. Explain the proposed form and openings and illustrate them in an external sketch. Other thoughtful modern or traditional designs are accepted: a flat roof, a particular material or every feature in the sample is not compulsory. These marks do not include the separately marked internal layout or garden connection.

rows.verbatim: the space is divided to provide some privacy and a sense of seclusion
rows.contextNote: Internal-layout notes 6 and sketches 6 (12 total). Join the extension to the south-facing rear wall M–M at A and keep the specified 5.0 m × 3.0 m internal space. The source describes a small desk/office area for individual work and a larger communal area, with separation giving privacy; a convertible couch is an optional example, not a required bedroom. Show a workable internal arrangement for the stated study and occasional family uses, with access and circulation related to the original plan. The source plan is illustrative: do not require its exact furniture arrangement or copy it at the expense of the printed dimensions. External form and garden-link marks are awarded in their own tasks.

Award the published shared 6-mark criterion for showing how the proposed space links to the rear garden. Join the extension to the south-facing rear wall M–M at A and keep the specified 5.0 m × 3.0 m internal space. Source examples include double, folding or sliding doors, glazing for garden views, and a patio giving outdoor seating and access. Show a coherent indoor/outdoor relationship appropriate to the selected location; the example doors/windows are alternatives and are not all mandatory. A covered connection to the house can be relevant to option B, but it does not replace the requested link to the garden. No separate notes/sketch split is printed for this 6-mark criterion.

rows.verbatim: increases use made of the valuable space outside
rows.contextNote: Award two distinct advantages at 3 marks each (6 total). The source examples include closer contact with nature, awareness of seasonal change, enjoyment of the senses, educational opportunities for children, access to natural light, more use of outside space, and a greater sense of spaciousness. Discuss the relationship between the new room and garden. Merely naming a door type describes a design feature, not its advantage. The menu is open; other relevant, well-argued benefits are accepted.

questionRef: 2015 HL Q4(a) — respect for local character
stem: An old house built in the vernacular tradition is to be eco-refurbished. Part (a) selects any TWO of respect for local character, breathable structure and reuse of materials. For part (b), one cottage in the illustrated row of single-storey cottages needs significant refurbishment. The survey finds an un-insulated traditional cut roof with natural slates; softwood windows, single-glazed with sliding sash; and an un-insulated suspended timber floor. Select any TWO of these three areas and use notes and freehand sketches to describe upgrading EACH selected area while respecting the appearance and character of the original cottages. The two selections in (a) and (b) are independent.
questionText: Discuss the importance of respect for local character in the eco-refurbishment of the old vernacular house.

rows.verbatim: vernacular architecture evolved from its location
rows.contextNote: This is one published 10-mark discussion criterion. The scheme does not divide it into a fixed number of separately marked points; do not invent point-by-point marks. Relevant, developed discussion is required and other relevant information is acceptable. Explain the relationship between the house, local materials and labour, simple traditional scale/detailing, neighbouring cottages and landscape. Plan the work to conserve that historical character and the unity of the row while improving the building fabric and reducing energy demand. The source recommends a considered approach specific to the building and conservation advice; it does not require every example or one universal refurbishment formula.

questionText: Discuss the importance of a breathable structure in the eco-refurbishment of the old vernacular house.

rows.verbatim: a breathable structure allows the gradual movement of moisture
rows.contextNote: This is one published 10-mark discussion criterion. The scheme does not divide it into a fixed number of separately marked points; do not invent point-by-point marks. Relevant, developed discussion is required and other relevant information is acceptable. Explain how suitable permeable fabric and hygroscopic materials allow moisture movement and drying rather than trapping water in traditional walls and roof, reducing surface/interstitial condensation risk. questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, describe the steps in upgrading the un-insulated traditional cut roof with natural slates while respecting the original cottage appearance and character.

rows.verbatim: the repair is to retain as far as possible the historic fabric of the roof
rows.contextNote: Award notes 10 and freehand sketches 10, total 20, for this selected area. The rubric publishes no finer per-step subdivision. Both the upgrading sequence and respect for the original cottage character are required; a written list alone does not earn sketch marks. Survey and retain sound roof timbers; number and store slates, repair decayed rafter ends/wallplate where necessary using compatible material, and reinstate original or matching slates, fascia and soffit profiles. Show an appropriate insulated roof assembly, membrane and ventilation/moisture strategy with continuity at the wallplate. The source gives breathable insulation arrangements and, separately, a warm-side continuous vapour barrier with service cavity; these are alternative coherent designs, not cumulative mandatory layers. Do not require every illustrated insulation type or claim that a vapour barrier is forbidden in all designs. The source panel retains both examples.

questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, describe the steps in upgrading the single-glazed softwood sliding sash windows while respecting the original cottage appearance and character.

rows.verbatim: maintenance and repair of historic windows is recommended before replacement
rows.contextNote: Award notes 10 and freehand sketches 10, total 20, for this selected area. The rubric publishes no finer per-step subdivision. Both the upgrading sequence and respect for the original cottage character are required; a written list alone does not earn sketch marks. Survey, record and number the sashes/glass; remove and repair damaged timber with compatible species/profiles, prepare and repaint, and reinstate serviceable glazing. Check cords, pulleys and ironmongery. Explain and sketch a suitable thermal/draught improvement: appropriate sash seals and glazing where rebates permit, or discreet internally fitted secondary glazing. Preserve glazing-bar proportions, profiles and external appearance. The scheme presents repair, re-glazing and secondary glazing as alternatives; do not require all options simultaneously or default to replacing sound historic windows. Where secondary glazing is chosen, retain a coherent moisture/ventilation arrangement.

questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, describe the steps in upgrading the un-insulated suspended timber floor while respecting the original cottage appearance and character.

rows.contextNote: Award notes 10 and freehand sketches 10, total 20, for this selected area. The rubric publishes no finer per-step subdivision. Both the upgrading sequence and respect for the original cottage character are required; a written list alone does not earn sketch marks. Establish the floor’s historical significance, record and number boards/skirtings, lift and store them carefully, inspect joists/boards and repair decayed parts. Preserve sub-floor ventilation. Show supported insulation fitted between joists without gaps, an appropriate breathable layer and reinstatement of the numbered boards/skirting. The source shows alternative insulation supports/assemblies, including netting for soft insulation or battens with board support; these are examples, not additional choose-one card routes. Retain the suspended floor rather than substituting an unrelated solid concrete floor. Source page 14 also contains adjacent window examples; only the floor treatment earns this task’s marks.

stem: The new house has a concrete-block external wall: 16 mm external render, 100 mm outer concrete-block leaf, a 250 mm cavity FULLY filled with polystyrene bead insulation, 100 mm inner concrete-block leaf and 12 mm internal plaster. Rse = 0.048 and Rsi = 0.122 m²·°C/W. Conductivities in W/(m·°C): render 0.720; both concrete-block leaves 1.440; polystyrene bead 0.031; plaster 0.220. For EACH house, external wall area is 150 m², average inside temperature 20 °C and outside 6 °C. Heating runs 8 hours/day, every day, for 35 weeks/year. Oil costs €0.95/litre and provides 37,350 kJ/litre; 1,000 W = 1 kJ/s. Part (a) calculates the new wall U-value; part (b) calculates annual wall heat-loss cost for BOTH the new house using (a) and an existing house with U = 0.21 W/(m²·°C). Part (c) details water exclusion at the new house’s window head. The existing-house compliance statement belongs to the 2015 paper, not a current regulatory claim.
questionText: Calculate the U-value of the specified full-fill insulated external wall of the new house, showing the component resistances, total resistance and U-value.

rows.contextNote: Use a clear resistance table or equivalent method. Convert layer thicknesses from mm to m; R = thickness/conductivity, add both surface resistances and all five material layers, then U = 1/Rtotal. The rubric heading “Insulated concrete ground floor” is a source error: the paper and the worked solution describe the specified external wall.

Two separately published checks at 3 marks each. Use the supplied external surface resistance Rse = 0.048 m²·°C/W directly; do not divide it by a thickness or conductivity. Use the supplied internal surface resistance Rsi = 0.122 m²·°C/W directly.

Five separately published material-resistance checks at 3 marks each; retain both concrete-block leaves. Rrender = 0.016/0.720 = 0.02222222 m²·°C/W. Router block = 0.100/1.440 = 0.06944444 m²·°C/W. The outer and inner block leaves each contribute their own resistance. Rbead = 0.250/0.031 = 8.06451613 m²·°C/W. The cavity is fully filled: do not add a separate air-cavity resistance. Rinner block = 0.100/1.440 = 0.06944444 m²·°C/W. Include this second leaf as well as the outer leaf. Rplaster = 0.012/0.220 = 0.05454545 m²·°C/W.

U = 1/Rtotal = 1/8.45017269 = 0.11834078 W/(m²·°C), approximately 0.1183 W/(m²·°C). The rubric awards 1 mark for the formula alone within this 3-mark criterion, not an additional mark. The remaining criteria stay at their own published 3-mark allocations.

stem: The new house has a traditional cut roof pitched at 45°, an internal width of 6.0 m and high roof insulation. Insulated plasterboard with skim finish is fixed under the rafters. The external supporting wall is 400 mm concrete block with a full-fill insulated cavity. The FLOOR joists are 225 mm × 40 mm and are supported centrally on a 100 mm internal load-bearing concrete-block wall. The attic floor finish is 25 mm tongue-and-groove boards. At scale 1:10, the vertical section passes through one half of the roof, eaves to ridge, showing one external wall and one rafter length, from 500 mm below the floor joists to the ridge. Include three courses of slate at the eaves and four typical roof dimensions. Part (b) adds ventilation details at BOTH eaves and roof/ridge.
questionText: To scale 1:10, draw the specified vertical section through half of the traditional cut roof, from 500 mm below floor joists to ridge. Include the external wall, one rafter length, three slate courses at eaves and four typical dimensions.

rows.verbatim: Vertical section through roof structure - attic
rows.contextNote: Award the best TEN acceptable construction details only: drawing 3 plus annotation 1 for each, maximum 40. Published examples are 400 mm external wall; full-fill cavity insulation; internal/external plaster/render; cavity closer;100 mm load-bearing centre wall; wallplate; rafter; insulated slab under rafter; vertical purlin; strut/collar; breather membrane/battens; counter-battens; slates; fascia/soffit/gutter(any TWO of these for ONE 4-mark criterion); ridge board; and joist/25 mm tongue-and-groove floorboards. Other appropriate detailing is accepted. Do not require all 16 indicative criteria or count the fascia/soffit/gutter as three separate 4-mark details. Preserve the paper’s 225×40 mm FLOOR joists; the scheme’s generic 200×40 mm ceiling-joist example does not replace the printed floor specification.

Include four appropriate typical dimensions for the specified roof section. This is the published 4-mark dimension allowance, separate from construction annotations and the scale/draughting marks; no finer partial band is printed. Keep the specified 45°pitch,6.0 m internal width,400 mm wall,225×40 mm floor joists and 100 mm centre support consistent.

Scale 1:10 earns the published 4-mark scale allowance. Draughting is 4 excellent,3 good or 2 fair; use 0 if no credit. The combined selectable totals are sums of scale 0/4 and draughting 0/2/3/4, giving 0,2,3,4,6,7,8. Do not award the same presentation marks again in (b).

stem: A wood-burning stove combined with a solar collector is to provide central heating AND hot water for a three-bedroom, two-storey dwelling house. The design must show two independently controlled heating zones, one on each floor, with three radiators on EACH floor, control-valve locations and typical pipe sizes. The solar collector is for water heating (solar thermal). Part (c) asks for two design considerations when selecting locations for BOTH the chimney and the hot press, using notes and freehand sketches and justifying the choices.
questionText: Using notes and a single-line diagram, show a typical layout for BOTH central heating and domestic hot water, supplied by the wood-burning stove combined with the solar collector. Show two independently controlled heating zones, one per floor, and three radiators on each floor. Locate control valves and give typical pipe sizes.

rows.contextNote: Award the best NINE acceptable system details, each sketch 3 plus annotation 1, capped at 36. The source menu includes stove; radiator flow/return; radiators; zone valves and thermostats; header/expansion/storage tank and feeds; expansion pipe/vessel; primary flow/return; pump/valves; solar collector, flow/return and pump; twin-coil cylinder; control panel; expansion and temperature-reducing vessels. Preserve both heat sources, two independently controlled zones and six radiators. For the optional pump/valves criterion, any two applicable radiator/isolating/drain-off components satisfy that ONE detail; do not award an extra 4 marks per item. Notes on the source diagram identify zone thermostats T1/T2 although the drawn labels repeat T2; retain two independent controls.

Two appropriate labelled pipe sizes at 2 marks each. Published examples: 22 mm flow/return, 15 mm upstands and 28 mm expansion. The 300-litre twin-coil cylinder and 230-litre cold-water store are capacities, NOT pipe diameters, and do not earn these pipe-size marks. Suitable alternative coherent system sizes are accepted; this is not a closed choose-two pool of three fixed answers.

questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, show a preferred location for the solar collector that will ensure its maximum efficiency in the specified water-heating system.

rows.contextNote: Explain a suitable unshaded location, normally facing south, with a coherent roof/ground/wall placement and appropriate tilt. The 2015 scheme gives a 45° optimum tilt and approximately 15° east/west tolerance as examples. Avoid chimney/tree shade and consider roof support, insulation and overheating. Its PV domestic-electricity statistic is unrelated to the required solar-thermal water-heating answer; do not substitute photovoltaic electricity generation.

Show the preferred location with a freehand sketch: collector orientation and an appropriate inclined installation, unobstructed sunlight and its relationship to the building. Keep the complete source orientation and tilt illustrations available. The awkward source phrase inclined to horizontal means an inclination relative to the horizontal, not a requirement to lay the collector flat.

questionText:
Using notes and a single-line diagram, show a typical layout for BOTH central heating and domestic hot water, supplied by the wood-burning stove combined with the solar collector. Show two independently controlled heating zones, one per floor, and three radiators on each floor. Locate control valves and give typical pipe sizes.

Using notes and freehand sketches, show a preferred location for the solar collector that will ensure its maximum efficiency in the specified water-heating system.

Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss two considerations that should be taken into account at the design stage when selecting a location for BOTH the chimney and the hot press. Justify your design choices.

rows.contextNote: Award the best NINE acceptable system details, each sketch 3 plus annotation 1, capped at 36. The source menu includes stove; radiator flow/return; radiators; zone valves and thermostats; header/expansion/storage tank and feeds; expansion pipe/vessel; primary flow/return; pump/valves; solar collector, flow/return and pump; twin-coil cylinder; control panel; expansion and temperature-reducing vessels. Preserve both heat sources, two independently controlled zones and six radiators. For the optional pump/valves criterion, any two applicable radiator/isolating/drain-off components satisfy that ONE detail; do not award an extra 4 marks per item. Notes on the source diagram identify zone thermostats T1/T2 although the drawn labels repeat T2; retain two independent controls.

Two appropriate labelled pipe sizes at 2 marks each. Published examples: 22 mm flow/return, 15 mm upstands and 28 mm expansion. The 300-litre twin-coil cylinder and 230-litre cold-water store are capacities, NOT pipe diameters, and do not earn these pipe-size marks. Suitable alternative coherent system sizes are accepted; this is not a closed choose-two pool of three fixed answers.

Explain a suitable unshaded location, normally facing south, with a coherent roof/ground/wall placement and appropriate tilt. The 2015 scheme gives a 45° optimum tilt and approximately 15° east/west tolerance as examples. Avoid chimney/tree shade and consider roof support, insulation and overheating. Its PV domestic-electricity statistic is unrelated to the required solar-thermal water-heating answer; do not substitute photovoltaic electricity generation.

Show the preferred location with a freehand sketch: collector orientation and an appropriate inclined installation, unobstructed sunlight and its relationship to the building. Keep the complete source orientation and tilt illustrations available. The awkward source phrase inclined to horizontal means an inclination relative to the horizontal, not a requirement to lay the collector flat.

stem: Design the external envelope of the two-storey house to be thermal bridge free. It has a 450 mm concrete-block external wall with a 250 mm full-fill insulated cavity, a traditional cut roof, tongue-and-groove first-floor boards on timber joists, and an insulated solid-concrete ground floor. The original diagram circles FOUR junctions: roof/wall at eaves; upper floor/external wall; window cill; ground floor/external wall. Part (a) selects any THREE of these four. A window head appears in the scheme commentary but is NOT a fifth circled option.
questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, show best-practice detailing that prevents a thermal bridge at the roof/wall junction at eaves. This is one 16-mark location from the printed choose-three task.

rows.contextNote: Continue the wall and roof insulation through the eaves junction rather than leaving a conductive gap. The source model includes 250 mm full-fill cavity insulation, a 60 mm cavity closer, AAC block, 60 mm rigid insulation board and 400 mm fibreglass insulation. Coordinate the eaves construction and required ventilation; do not bridge the insulation with a continuous conductive element. Award the published 8-mark notes allowance for this one selected location; the scheme prints no finer breakdown.

Draw and label a coherent section through the roof/wall junction at eaves, showing how the insulation remains continuous. Use the corresponding model illustration with the original house specification. This is the separate published 8-mark sketch allowance, not another notes allowance.

questionText: Discuss the importance of designing a building envelope that is thermal bridge free.

rows.verbatim: Discussion (point 1) - 2 marks for point, 4 marks for discussion
rows.contextNote: Give a distinct valid point (2) and develop its importance (4). Source-supported routes include reduced heat loss and heating demand; more even internal surface temperatures and comfort; less risk of cold surfaces reaching dew point, condensation and mould; less material deterioration and associated health effects. Explain the causal relationship, not just a label, and avoid repeating the other point. Thermal bridging is local increased conduction; airtightness alone does not remove every conductive bridge.

questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss in detail the importance of airtight building envelope in Passive House design. This is one of the two selected16-mark topics.

rows.contextNote: Explain a continuous airtight layer, carefully sealed junctions/penetrations and controlled fresh-air supply. The source examples include taped membranes, plaster continuity, service cavities and blower-door testing. Airtightness limits uncontrolled leakage; it does not eliminate conductive heat loss through the fabric. Do not confuse the airtight barrier with insulation, or omit deliberate ventilation.
Sketch an uninterrupted air-barrier line around the section and show continuity at a relevant junction or service penetration, as in the source red-line diagram.

Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss in detail the importance of space heating demand in Passive House design. This is one of the two selected16-mark topics.

Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of thermal mass in Passive House design.

Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the function of carefully designed solar shading for the Passive House shown.

rows.contextNote: Explain a continuous airtight layer, carefully sealed junctions/penetrations and controlled fresh-air supply. The source examples include taped membranes, plaster continuity, service cavities and blower-door testing. Airtightness limits uncontrolled leakage; it does not eliminate conductive heat loss through the fabric. Do not confuse the airtight barrier with insulation, or omit deliberate ventilation.
Sketch an uninterrupted air-barrier line around the section and show continuity at a relevant junction or service penetration, as in the source red-line diagram.

Explain the small energy demand for heating indoor spaces, distinguished from domestic hot water and total primary energy. The 2015 scheme cites space-heating demand ≤15 kWh/m² per year and heating load ≤10 W/m²; these are different quantities. Low fabric losses, controlled ventilation and useful gains reduce demand. Its primary-energy factor 2.58 and 120 kWh/m²/year criterion are historical scheme figures, not asserted as current rules.

Use a relevant freehand sketch to connect reduced fabric/ventilation losses and useful heat gains with the low space-heating demand. Label the mechanisms; do not treat a tariff number by itself as the required sketch.

Explain how exposed heavy materials absorb and store heat and release it later, moderating and delaying temperature peaks. The source examples include concrete floors/walls, brick and stone, with high density and heat capacity and suitable conductivity. Thermal mass must work with useful solar gain, shading and ventilation; it is not the same as thermal insulation.

Sketch solar radiation entering glazing, absorption/storage in the floor or wall and later heat release to the occupied space, as in the source model. Make the time-shifted storage/release mechanism clear.

Explain limiting excessive direct summer gain and glare while allowing useful winter sun. Source examples include correctly sized overhangs, brise-soleil, adjustable external screens, blinds and balconies without thermal bridges. Select and justify suitable design details for the illustrated house; do not treat the example list as a compulsory finite pool.

Sketch the chosen shading detail and the high summer/low winter sun paths, or the operation of adjustable shading, to explain the function. Retain the illustrated house as context and distinguish external interception of sunlight from internal blinds. The source provides several complete alternative model drawings.

stem: This is the ALTERNATIVE Question 10, based on the original printed passage adapted from Dermot Bannon, LOVE YOUR HOME: Secrets to a Successful Space (2014), Gill & Macmillan, ISBN 9780717164486. Read the complete passage in the attached original question. It discusses the role of light in architecture and wellbeing, changing glass technology, the limited daylight in many older Irish homes, lower-U-value glazing and the attraction of natural light. Discuss the statement, explain glazing advances and recommend THREE best-practice daylight guidelines. The passage’s description of glazing without heat loss is qualitative rhetoric: a low U-value reduces heat loss rather than eliminating it. This alternative is a single 60-mark route, not an addition to the primary Passive House question.
questionText: Discuss the original printed statement about light, architecture and the changing use of glazing in detail.

rows.verbatim: Discussion – point 1 (3 for point, 5 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Develop one distinct, relevant point from the passage: the importance of daylight for the quality and use of spaces; the changing architectural possibilities of glass; the contrast with older limited/draughty glazing; orientation and room layout; the relationship between light, views and occupants. Award point 3 and discussion 5, without repeating another point. Discuss the qualitative passage critically: lower U-values reduce heat loss, rather than making it zero. Historical commentary is not a current-law claim.

questionText: Outline how advances in glazing technology have led to increased use of glass in house design, in the context of the printed passage.

rows.verbatim: Advances in glazing technology - increased use of glass
rows.contextNote: Explain relevant improvements and their design consequences, for example low-emissivity coatings reducing radiant heat transfer, insulating/vacuum glazing, safer laminated or structural glazing, or controllable tint. This is one shared 6-mark allowance; the scheme does not publish a separate mark per technology. The source’s claim that low iron content itself reduces conductivity is not used as a required technical explanation. Lower U-values permit reduced heat loss; they do not mean no heat transfer at all.

stem: A front porch with a tiled roof is shown in the sketch. The porch has an internal width of 2.0 metres. The roof of the porch, which is insulated, is a traditional cut roof and has a pitch of 30°. The roof is supported on a 400 mm concrete block wall with a 200 mm full-fill insulated cavity. The rafters and ceiling joists are 200 mm × 40 mm. Insulated plasterboard is also fixed to the underside of the ceiling joists.
questionText: To a scale of 1:5, draw a vertical section through one half of the roof of the porch, to show one rafter length. Show the typical construction details from a level 400 mm below the wallplate, through the wall and eaves up to the ridge. Show three courses of tiles at eaves. Include four typical dimensions. Note: It is not necessary to show the front door.

rows.verbatim: Any 9 of the above details (4 marks each)
rows.contextNote: Credit the best NINE acceptable details at 4 marks each, capped at 36. Published examples include ridge board; concrete tiles; battens; overlapped/taped breather membrane; rafters; roof insulation; ceiling joists; insulated plasterboard; wallplate; internal plaster; inner block leaf; full-fill cavity insulation; outer block leaf; external plaster; soffit/fascia; eaves gutter. Preserve the printed 200×40 mm rafters/ceiling joists, 400 mm wall and 200 mm cavity. The source does not divide these 4-mark details into drawing3/annotation1; do not import that Higher-level allocation. The full indicative menu is not mandatory.

Include four appropriate dimensions for the specified roof section. This is the published shared 4-mark dimension allowance; no finer partial allocation is printed. Keep the given 30° pitch, 2.0 m internal width and component sizes consistent. The separate whole-drawing quality allowance is not included again here.

questionRef: 2015 OL Q2(a) — filling the cavity with insulation
stem: The sketch shows a dwelling house which was built over 40 years ago. The external wall is a 300 mm concrete block wall with a 100 mm cavity. There is no insulation in the cavity. It is proposed to insulate the external wall by: filling the cavity with insulation and adding an external system of insulation to the wall.
questionText: It is proposed to insulate the external wall by: filling the cavity with insulation. Using notes and freehand sketches, show the steps to be followed in applying each system of insulation to the wall.

rows.verbatim: Filling the cavity with insulation – Notes
rows.contextNote: Three valid steps, 4 marks each. Typical procedure (carried out by specialist firms): 22 mm diameter holes are drilled through the external leaf, usually spaced about 800 mm horizontally and 1350 mm vertically; special care is taken at damp proof courses and at heads of windows and doors, with extra holes drilled around openings so the cavity fills properly; polystyrene beads are pumped into the cavity while a light coating of glue is applied, setting into a solid structure; when pumping is complete the holes are filled. Other valid steps are acceptable.

rows.verbatim: Filling the cavity with insulation – Sketches
rows.contextNote: Quality of sketches for the cavity-fill steps: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4. The scheme sketches show the drill entering the outer leaf and the hole spacing on the wall.

sourceMaterial.attribution: SEC Leaving Certificate Construction Studies 2015 Ordinary Level — © State Examinations Commission.
sourceMaterial.presentationNote: Both insulation systems are required: each keeps its own published notes and sketch marks. The scheme procedures are typical model answers, not the only acceptable sequence.

questionRef: 2015 OL Q2(a) — adding an external system of insulation
stem: The sketch shows a dwelling house which was built over 40 years ago. The external wall is a 300 mm concrete block wall with a 100 mm cavity. There is no insulation in the cavity. It is proposed to insulate the external wall by: filling the cavity with insulation and adding an external system of insulation to the wall.
questionText: It is proposed to insulate the external wall by: adding an external system of insulation to the wall. Using notes and freehand sketches, show the steps to be followed in applying each system of insulation to the wall.

rows.verbatim: Adding an external system of insulation to the wall – Notes
rows.contextNote: Three valid steps, 4 marks each. Typical procedure: the first row of insulation boards is fixed in place resting on a stainless steel track; boards are fixed in position with a special adhesive, and all rows are fixed and the adhesive allowed to set; mechanical fixings (typically about seven per square metre, longer for thicker boards) are installed by drilling through the insulation into the wall and then hammered into place. Typical insulation materials: polystyrene, mineral fibre board, wood fibre board. Other valid steps are acceptable.

rows.verbatim: Adding an external system of insulation to the wall – Sketches
rows.contextNote: Quality of sketches for the external-insulation steps: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4. The scheme sketch shows the wall, adhesive, insulation board and mechanical fixing.

Typical procedure (carried out by specialist firms): 22 mm diameter holes are drilled through the external leaf, usually spaced about 800 mm horizontally and 1350 mm vertically; special care is taken at damp proof courses and at heads of windows and doors, with extra holes drilled around openings so the cavity fills properly; polystyrene beads are pumped into the cavity while a light coating of glue is applied, setting into a solid structure; when pumping is complete the holes are filled. Other valid steps are acceptable.

rows.verbatim: Filling the cavity with insulation – Sketches
rows.contextNote: Quality of sketches for the cavity-fill steps: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4. The scheme sketches show the drill entering the outer leaf and the hole spacing on the wall.

rows.verbatim: Adding an external system of insulation to the wall – Notes
rows.contextNote: Three valid steps, 4 marks each. Typical procedure: the first row of insulation boards is fixed in place resting on a stainless steel track; boards are fixed in position with a special adhesive, and all rows are fixed and the adhesive allowed to set; mechanical fixings (typically about seven per square metre, longer for thicker boards) are installed by drilling through the insulation into the wall and then hammered into place. Typical insulation materials: polystyrene, mineral fibre board, wood fibre board. Other valid steps are acceptable.

rows.verbatim: Adding an external system of insulation to the wall – Sketches
rows.contextNote: Quality of sketches for the external-insulation steps: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4. The scheme sketch shows the wall, adhesive, insulation board and mechanical fixing.

questionText: Discuss two advantages of insulating the external walls of the house.

rows.verbatim: Two advantages of insulating the external walls of the house
rows.contextNote: Two distinct advantages, 5 marks each, discussed rather than just named. stem: A water butt is used to collect rainwater from the pitched roof of a house, as shown.
questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, show the pipework necessary to collect the rainwater from the roof and to store it in the water butt.

rows.verbatim: pipework necessary to collect and store rainwater from the roof

stem: A water butt is used to collect rainwater from the pitched roof of a house, as shown.
questionText: Discuss two advantages of using a water butt to store rainwater.

rows.verbatim: Two advantages of using a water butt to store rainwater
rows.contextNote: Two distinct advantages, 5 marks each. Such as: environmentally friendly, reducing the amount of treated water used; lower water bills where meters are installed; rainwater is satisfactory for watering gardens and washing cars; butts are inexpensive, easy to fit and maintain, and can be linked in series for more storage.

stem: A water butt is used to collect rainwater from the pitched roof of a house, as shown.
questionText: Discuss two disadvantages of using a water butt to store rainwater.

questionText: Discuss two reasons why it is advisable to harvest rainwater.

rows.verbatim: Two reasons why it is advisable to harvest rainwater

rows.contextNote: Explain the natural seasoning with notes and freehand sketches; the main relevant explanation earns up to 6. Such as: a traditional method of reducing the moisture content of timber; planks are stacked parallel with spaces between, separated by stickers (usually about 25 mm × 15 mm), in an open shed on a clean, dry, level base such as brick piers, and dried by the prevailing weather; plank ends are painted to prevent splitting; one species per stack; moisture content falls to about 18–22%, in equilibrium with the surrounding air; cheap because it uses no electrical energy, but slow and the rate cannot be controlled. questionRef: 2015 OL Q8 — complete: triple glazing, solar panel, skirting board, compression fitting, concrete lintel
questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: triple glazing; solar panel; skirting board; compression fitting; concrete lintel.

rows.contextNote: Explain the triple glazing with notes and freehand sketches; the main relevant explanation earns up to 6. Such as: three panes of glass with a cavity between each; a better insulator and better acoustic performance than double glazing; low-e coatings reflect heat back into the house; cavities filled with argon or krypton reduce heat loss; an improved window U-value, a more comfortable indoor temperature and reduced condensation. A sketch should show the three panes, spacers and cavities.
Further relevant information about the triple glazing, in notes or sketches, earns up to 4. The scheme does not reserve fixed marks for notes versus sketches.

Explain the solar panel with notes and freehand sketches; the main relevant explanation earns up to 6. Such as: a solar collector absorbs solar radiation and converts it to heat, usually on a south-facing roof or secure ground-level fixing, working with other forms of heating and reducing CO2 emissions; types include flat-plate and evacuated-tube collectors, and tubes can be mounted to follow the sun. The scheme also lists photovoltaic panels: a coherent explanation of either is acceptable, but a photovoltaic panel produces electricity, not heat.
Further relevant information about the solar panel, in notes or sketches, earns up to 4. The scheme does not reserve fixed marks for notes versus sketches.

Explain the skirting board with notes and freehand sketches; the main relevant explanation earns up to 6. Such as: a decorative board fitted at the junction of a wall and floor, giving a neat finish; hardwood, softwood or MDF in various lengths and profiles; typical sections from 100 mm × 15 mm to 200 mm × 20 mm; mitred at internal and external corners. A sketch should show the board fixed at the wall–floor junction.
Further relevant information about the skirting board, in notes or sketches, earns up to 4. The scheme does not reserve fixed marks for notes versus sketches.

Explain the compression fitting with notes and freehand sketches; the main relevant explanation earns up to 6. Such as: a plumbing joint for copper or PVC pipes, made of brass or PVC in a range of sizes; the pipe ends are cut square, the nut and olive are fitted over the pipe, the pipe is pushed into the fitting and the nut is tightened to compress the olive into a watertight joint; PTFE tape may be used. A sketch should show the body, nut, olive and pipe.
Further relevant information about the compression fitting, in notes or sketches, earns up to 4. The scheme does not reserve fixed marks for notes versus sketches.

Explain the concrete lintel with notes and freehand sketches; the main relevant explanation earns up to 6. Such as: a reinforced concrete beam spanning a door or window opening, carrying the blockwork or brickwork above and transferring the load to the wall at either side; cast in situ or, more commonly, pre-stressed; the length depends on the opening width and the imposed loads, and pre-stressed lintels come in a range of lengths and widths. A sketch should show the lintel bearing on the wall either side of the opening.
Further relevant information about the concrete lintel, in notes or sketches, earns up to 4. The scheme does not reserve fixed marks for notes versus sketches.

Such as: battery operated with rechargeable batteries, so not directly connected to AC mains power in use; features similar to a mains drill, including hammer action; used for driving screws, with a clutch to prevent damage to screw heads; right-angle versions for tight spaces; several power and speed settings, light low-voltage drills for DIY and heavier higher-voltage drills for robust work. A sketch should show the drill body, chuck and battery.
Further relevant information about the cordless drill, in notes or sketches, earns up to 4. The scheme does not reserve fixed marks for notes versus sketches.

Explain the compression fitting with notes and freehand sketches; the main relevant explanation earns up to 6. Such as: a plumbing joint for copper or PVC pipes, made of brass or PVC in a range of sizes; the pipe ends are cut square, the nut and olive are fitted over the pipe, the pipe is pushed into the fitting and the nut is tightened to compress the olive into a watertight joint; PTFE tape may be used. A sketch should show the body, nut, olive and pipe.
Further relevant information about the compression fitting, in notes or sketches, earns up to 4. The scheme does not reserve fixed marks for notes versus sketches.

Explain the natural seasoning with notes and freehand sketches; the main relevant explanation earns up to 6. Such as: a traditional method of reducing the moisture content of timber; planks are stacked parallel with spaces between, separated by stickers (usually about 25 mm × 15 mm), in an open shed on a clean, dry, level base such as brick piers, and dried by the prevailing weather; plank ends are painted to prevent splitting; one species per stack; moisture content falls to about 18–22%, in equilibrium with the surrounding air; cheap because it uses no electrical energy, but slow and the rate cannot be controlled. A sketch should show the stacked planks, stickers and cover.
Further relevant information about the natural seasoning, in notes or sketches, earns up to 4. The scheme does not reserve fixed marks for notes versus sketches.

Explain the concrete lintel with notes and freehand sketches; the main relevant explanation earns up to 6. Such as: a reinforced concrete beam spanning a door or window opening, carrying the blockwork or brickwork above and transferring the load to the wall at either side; cast in situ or, more commonly, pre-stressed; the length depends on the opening width and the imposed loads, and pre-stressed lintels come in a range of lengths and widths. A sketch should show the lintel bearing on the wall either side of the opening.
Further relevant information about the concrete lintel, in notes or sketches, earns up to 4. The scheme does not reserve fixed marks for notes versus sketches.

Explain the radon barrier with notes and freehand sketches; the main relevant explanation earns up to 6. Such as: a flexible membrane placed under the floor and extended through the external walls to prevent radon gas entering the building; fitted over the whole floor area as one complete, unbroken layer with all joints taped and sealed, including around service pipes; usually laid over sand blinding (which protects it) and beneath the insulation; it replaces the damp proof membrane; installed with care by trained personnel so it is not damaged. Only a membrane rated and detailed as a radon barrier does this job.
Further relevant information about the radon barrier, in notes or sketches, earns up to 4. The scheme does not reserve fixed marks for notes versus sketches.

stem: The sketch shows portion of a wooden table. The table is designed for outdoor use.
questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, show a suitable joint for attaching one of the rail to the leg of the table. Give one reason for choosing this joint.

rows.contextNote: Name and describe a suitable joint, 4 marks. The scheme model is a haunched mortise and tenon: a mortise is removed from the top of the leg, the end of the rail is cut and shaped as a tenon to fit it, and a haunch formed on the tenon fits a matching recess, preventing the rail twisting and increasing the gluing surface. Any other suitable joint is acceptable.

questionText: Recommend a suitable finish for the table. Describe, using notes and freehand sketches, the steps involved in preparing the wood and in applying the recommended finish to the tabletop.

stem: The sketch shows a dwelling house with a traditional slated cut roof. The roof has a pitch of 30° and is highly insulated at ceiling joist level. The internal span of the house is 5.8 metres. The walls of the house are of 450 mm rendered concrete block construction with a full-fill insulated cavity.
questionText: To a scale of 1:10, draw a vertical section through one half of the roof structure, from just below eaves up to the ridge. Show one external wall and one rafter length. Include the typical construction details from 600 mm below the ceiling joists up to the ridge, and include three courses of slate at eaves. Include four typical dimensions.

rows.contextNote: Three external-wall details, 4 each (3 for drawing, 1 for annotation). Typical: external and internal render; 100 mm external and internal block leaves; wall ties; 250 mm full-fill insulated cavity; cavity closer; 100 mm × 75 mm wallplate(s).

Four roof-structure details, 4 each (3 drawing, 1 annotation). Typical: 200 mm × 50 mm rafters at 400 mm centres; ceiling joists at 400 mm centres; 225 mm × 75 mm purlin; strut supporting the purlin; hanger; collar tie at each couple or at 1200 mm centres; ridge board; plasterboard with 350 mm insulation laid in three layers.

Four eaves details, 4 each (3 drawing, 1 annotation). Typical: tilting fillet; fascia board, soffit and gutter (any two); 25 mm fascia ventilator and 50 mm proprietary eaves ventilator; wind-tightness barrier; breather membrane laid over the rafters; 50 mm × 30 mm slating battens; three courses of slates.
Four appropriate typical dimensions on the section.
Scale 4 and drafting 4, assessed together: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4.

stem: Lifetime use of a dwelling should be a key consideration at the design stage.
questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss two best-practice guidelines that should be followed when designing for lifetime use at each of the following areas of a dwelling: entrance access.

rows.contextNote: First guideline for the entrance access: notes 4 and sketches 4. Such as: a level threshold (maximum 15 mm upstand, chamfered or rounded edges) with a recessed drainage channel and the internal floor flush; a 1000 mm minimum clear door opening; a slip-resistant approach path at 1:20 or flatter (ramps no steeper than 1:12, with level landings); a level landing of at least 1500 mm × 1500 mm outside the door and 300 mm clear space at the leading edge; a canopy or recess at least 900 mm deep; lever handles 800–1050 mm above floor level and low door-closer force; a vision panel; motion-sensor lighting.
Second, different guideline for the entrance access: notes 4 and sketches 4. Do not credit the same guideline twice.

Consideration at the design stage is to be given to: creating an open-plan kitchen/dining and living space; optimising daylight; retaining a bedroom and family bathroom on the ground floor.

rows.verbatim: Create an open-plan kitchen/dining and living area

rows.verbatim: Optimising daylight into the ground floor

stem: The drawing shows the front elevation and ground floor plan of a farmhouse built in the 1920’s. The wall A-A is south-facing and the wall B-B is load-bearing. The owners wish to build a single-storey extension, no greater than 15 m² in area, to increase and revise the ground floor layout. Consideration at the design stage is to be given to: creating an open-plan kitchen/dining and living space; optimising daylight; retaining a bedroom and family bathroom on the ground floor.
questionText: Discuss three reasons for your proposed design layout.

rows.contextNote: Point 3 and discussion 4. Such as: environmental performance and passive solar gain from the south-facing wall A-A, with light reaching deep into the plan.
Point 3 and discussion 4. Such as: functional zoning and social connection in one open space, with no wasted hallway.

Point 3 and discussion 4. Such as: privacy and acoustic separation of the bedroom wing; services grouped near existing plumbing; ground-floor bedroom and bathroom for lifetime use. Three distinct reasons are needed.

stem: The sketch shows a railway keepers cottage built over 130 years ago. These traditional cottages can be seen at railway crossing points throughout our rural landscape. They form an important part of our built heritage.
questionText: A survey of the cottage reveals: 500 mm solid external wall of stone construction, uninsulated, with an internal lime render. Using notes and freehand sketches, describe in detail the steps involved in upgrading the thermal performance of each area selected in a manner that respects the original character of the cottage.

rows.verbatim: Steps involved in upgrading the thermal performance of each area selected
rows.contextNote: Notes on the steps for the stone wall, respecting the cottage’s character. Such as: keep the wall breathable, with layers more vapour-permeable towards the outside and no impermeable vapour barriers; use hygroscopic natural insulation (hemp/hempcrete, lime, wood fibre, cork, sheep’s wool); rake out and repoint with lime mortar by hand (joints raked to twice their width, dampened first, filled in stages, protected with hessian while it carbonates); apply hempcrete internally and allow 4–6 weeks to dry, then lime render, or a three-coat lime plaster (scud coat, haired scratch coat, float coat, lime-putty finish).
Sketches showing the upgrade steps and construction for the stone wall.

stem: The sketch shows a railway keepers cottage built over 130 years ago. These traditional cottages can be seen at railway crossing points throughout our rural landscape. They form an important part of our built heritage.
questionText: A survey of the cottage reveals: uninsulated traditional cut roof with natural slate. Using notes and freehand sketches, describe in detail the steps involved in upgrading the thermal performance of each area selected in a manner that respects the original character of the cottage.

rows.verbatim: Steps involved in upgrading the thermal performance of each area selected
rows.contextNote: Notes on the steps for the cut roof, respecting the cottage’s character. Such as: remove and set aside the slates, cleaning only their undersides; check and repair decayed rafters, wallplate and fascia in the same species and profile with traditional joints; treat new timber (boron); fit a vapour-permeable breathable membrane with counter-battens for ventilation; insulate with hygroscopic materials (sheep’s wool between rafters, wood fibre board above or below); keep the roof ventilated; re-lay the slates with the heaviest at the eaves, replacing broken ones with reclaimed slate; period cast-iron rainwater goods.
Sketches showing the upgrade steps and construction for the cut roof.

stem: The sketch shows a railway keepers cottage built over 130 years ago. These traditional cottages can be seen at railway crossing points throughout our rural landscape. They form an important part of our built heritage.
questionText: A survey of the cottage reveals: single-glazed, softwood sliding sash windows. Using notes and freehand sketches, describe in detail the steps involved in upgrading the thermal performance of each area selected in a manner that respects the original character of the cottage.

rows.verbatim: Steps involved in upgrading the thermal performance of each area selected
rows.contextNote: Notes on the steps for the sash windows, respecting the cottage’s character. Such as: repair rather than replace the original sashes, using a specialist conservation joiner; remove sashes and glass carefully, recording positions; replace only rotten timber in the same species and profiles with traditional joints and animal glue; free the pulleys, renew the sash cords and reuse the weights; reglaze with linseed-oil putty (salvaged or sourced float glass); repaint with non-toxic paint; add discreet secondary glazing to cut heat loss; record the repair.
Sketches showing the upgrade steps and construction for the sash windows.

stem: Shown in the sketch is the proposed external wall design detail for a new house of timber frame construction.
questionText: Calculate the U-value of the proposed wall, given the construction has the following sequence and data: External render thickness 16 mm External concrete block thickness 100 mm Clear cavity width 60 mm Oriented Strand Board (OSB) thickness 12 mm Timber stud thickness 250 mm Insulation between studs thickness 250 mm Oriented Strand Board (OSB) thickness 12 mm Plasterboard thickness 12.5 mm. Thermal data of the external wall: Resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m2 ºC/W; Resistivity of external render (r) 2.170 m ºC/W; Conductivity of concrete block (k) 1.440 W/m ºC; Resistance of clear cavity (R) 0.440 m2 ºC/W; Conductivity of OSB (k) 0.130 W/m ºC; Conductivity of insulation (k) 0.039 W/m ºC; Conductivity of OSB (k) 0.130 W/m ºC; Conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.250 W/m ºC; Resistance of internal surface (R) 0.130 m2 ºC/W. Note: The timber studs need not be considered in your calculations.

rows.contextNote: Set out the layers, thicknesses (in metres), k or r values and resistances in a table.
External surface resistance 0.048 and internal surface resistance 0.130 m²°C/W, 3 each.

Seven layer resistances, 3 each: render 0.016 × 2.170 = 0.035; concrete block 0.100 ÷ 1.440 = 0.069; clear cavity 0.440 (given); OSB 0.012 ÷ 0.130 = 0.092; insulation 0.250 ÷ 0.039 = 6.410; OSB 0.092; plasterboard 0.0125 ÷ 0.250 = 0.050 m²°C/W. The studs are ignored, as the question states.
Total resistance Rt = 7.367 m²°C/W (sum of all resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 7.367 = 0.136 W/m²°C, with units.

sourceMaterial.title: Timber-frame wall: U-value, heat-loss cost and moisture
sourceMaterial.attribution: SEC Leaving Certificate Construction Studies 2026 Higher Level — © State Examinations Commission.
sourceMaterial.presentationNote: All printed data are retained in the original question. Part (b) uses the U-value from part (a); the scheme’s worked answers are U = 0.136 W/m²°C and an annual cost of €40.27.

stem: Shown in the sketch is the proposed external wall design detail for a new house of timber frame construction.
questionText: Using the U-value of the wall obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through this wall: area of external wall 144 m2; average internal temperature 20 ºC; average external temperature 7 ºC; heating period 6 hours daily for 33 weeks per annum; cost of wood pellets 55 cent per kg; calorific value of wood pellets 17350 kJ per kg; 1000 watts 1 kJ per second.

rows.contextNote: Heat loss = U × area × temperature difference = 0.136 × 144 × (20 − 7) = 254.592 W (J/s).
Heating time = 60 × 60 × 6 × 7 × 33 = 4,989,600 seconds per year.

rows.verbatim: Kgs of wood pellets for one year
rows.contextNote: Wood pellets = 1,270,312.243 ÷ 17,350 = 73.2168 kg per year.
Cost = 73.2168 × €0.55 = €40.27 per year. The single-formula method (U × area × ΔT × seconds × cost ÷ (calorific value × 1000)) gives the same €40.27.

stem: A continuous thermal envelope is essential to prevent thermal bridging in a dwelling. The drawing shows a vertical section through the external leaf of a bungalow having a 450 mm concrete block wall with a 250 mm full-fill insulated cavity. The house has a truss roof and an insulated concrete ground floor. The window frame is thermally broken.
questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, show best practice design detailing that will prevent the formation of a thermal bridge at locations circled on the drawing — wall and roof junction

rows.contextNote: Notes on best-practice detailing at the circled wall and roof junction. Such as: wall and roof insulation meeting to keep the envelope continuous; a thermal break at the wallplate (insulated barrier or thermal blocks); cavity insulation continued and the eaves detailed to avoid a cold bridge; no direct structural or steel connections bridging the insulation.
Sketches of the wall and roof junction detail showing the continuous insulation line.

stem: EnerPHit is a certified standard that can be achieved when retrofitting an older house to improve its energy efficiency. The sketch shows a bungalow which has been retrofitted to the EnerPHit Passive House standard.
questionText: Select any three areas of the building fabric of an older house that would need to be retrofitted to achieve the EnerPHit Passive House standard. Give a reason for each area selected.

rows.contextNote: Area 1 and its reason (1 + 5). Such as: external walls — external wall insulation or pumped cavity bead to cut the U-value and junction thermal bridges.
Area 2 and its reason (1 + 5). Such as: ground floor — sub-floor insulation under a new slab; or the roof/attic — 400 mm+ insulation.

Area 3 and its reason (1 + 5). Such as: windows and doors — triple-glazed, airtight units; the airtightness layer — sealed membrane and tapes for a low air-change rate; thermal-bridge elimination at junctions. Three distinct areas are needed.

stem: “It would be reasonable to assume that ensuring good indoor air quality would be a key factor when designing and constructing buildings. The term sick building syndrome became well known in the 1980’s and still lingers today, though largely associated with poorly air-conditioned offices. However, the health impacts of buildings are still poorly understood and rarely taken into account as a key priority when buildings are designed or renovated. Architects, when specifying building materials are mainly concerned with cost, availability, robustness and aesthetics, not their impacts on health.” Adapted from: Building Materials, Health and Indoor Air Quality: No Breathing Space by Tom Wooley
questionText: Discuss the above statement in detail.

rows.contextNote: Point 5 and discussion 5. Such as: people spend most of their lives indoors, yet health is often overlooked behind cost, appearance, durability and availability; sick building syndrome symptoms linked to poor ventilation, mould and chemical emissions.

Point 5 and discussion 5. Such as: more airtight buildings need carefully designed ventilation; VOCs and formaldehyde from paints, adhesives, finishes and composite boards; condensation and mould from poor detailing, especially in Ireland’s damp climate.

Point 5 and discussion 5. Such as: health impacts are harder to measure and appear later, while healthier materials can cost more; Passive House/EnerPHit ventilation with heat recovery, low-VOC materials, daylight and newer certification standards show a growing focus on wellbeing. Three distinct, well-argued points are needed.

stem: The sketch shows the external wooden door of a dwelling house. The external wall is a 400 mm concrete block wall with a full-fill insulated cavity which is plastered on both sides. rows.contextNote: Credit the best SEVEN acceptable details at 5 marks each, capped at 35. questionRef: 2026 OL Q8 — complete: triple glazing, ball valve, cordless circular saw, fascia board, smart meter
questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: triple glazing; ball valve; cordless circular saw; fascia board; smart meter.

rows.contextNote: Explain the triple glazing with notes and freehand sketches; the main relevant explanation earns up to 6. Such as: three panes of glass separated by insulating gaps, often argon-filled; more energy efficient than single or double glazing; high thermal and sound insulation; typically dearer than double glazing.
Further relevant information about the triple glazing, in notes or sketches, earns up to 4. The scheme does not reserve fixed marks for notes versus sketches.

Explain the ball valve with notes and freehand sketches; the main relevant explanation earns up to 6. Such as: controls flow with a rotating ball with a hole through it; open when the hole lines up with the pipe, closed when it is at right angles; the handle shows open, closed or partly open; used to isolate plumbing for maintenance or emergencies.
Further relevant information about the ball valve, in notes or sketches, earns up to 4. The scheme does not reserve fixed marks for notes versus sketches.

Explain the cordless circular saw with notes and freehand sketches; the main relevant explanation earns up to 6. Such as: a portable battery-powered (usually lithium-ion) saw for cutting wood, and sometimes metal or plastic, without a mains cable; can make rip, cross and bevel cuts.
Further relevant information about the cordless circular saw, in notes or sketches, earns up to 4. The scheme does not reserve fixed marks for notes versus sketches.

Explain the fascia board with notes and freehand sketches; the main relevant explanation earns up to 6. Such as: a horizontal board fixed to the ends of the rafters along the lower edge of the roof; timber or uPVC; protects the rafter ends and supports the gutter; closes the roof against moisture and pests; available in colours and decorative profiles.
Further relevant information about the fascia board, in notes or sketches, earns up to 4. The scheme does not reserve fixed marks for notes versus sketches.

Explain the smart meter with notes and freehand sketches; the main relevant explanation earns up to 6. Such as: an electricity meter that records use automatically and sends readings to the supplier, ending manual and estimated readings; splits use into day, night and peak times; shows usage patterns to help choose a tariff and save energy.
Further relevant information about the smart meter, in notes or sketches, earns up to 4. The scheme does not reserve fixed marks for notes versus sketches.
